Sub-events.Sub-event: Initial Plans for VIII Corps in Brittany
Sub-events.Sub-event_summary: Long-planned turn of VIII Corps into Brittany at Avranches, with orders from Bradley to Patton to seize key locations and clear the peninsula, alerting Communications Zone for port development.

Sub-event_fulltext.Paragraph_33: It had long been planned to turn the VIII Corps westward into Brittany as soon as the Americans reached the base of the Cotentin at Avranches. In moving toward Rennes and St. Malo, VIII Corps was to precede other units of the Third Army, which would clear the "whole of the Brittany Peninsula."<sup>[28](https://www.ibiblio.org/hyperwar/USA/USA-E-Breakout/fn18.html#fn28)</sup> General Bradley thus ordered Patton to drive south from Pontaubault to seize Rennes and Fougeres, then turn westward to secure St. Malo, the Quiberon Bay area, Brest, and the remainder of Brittany, in that sequence. The Communications Zone was alerted to the task of opening and developing the ports of St. Malo, Quiberon Bay, and Brest as soon as possible after their capture.<sup>[29](https://www.ibiblio.org/hyperwar/USA/USA-E-Breakout/fn18.html#fn29)</sup>

Sub-events.Sub-event: Adjustment of Forces Due to German Disorganization
Sub-events.Sub-event_summary: Pre-invasion plans for sizable U.S. force reduced due to German disorganization, allowing smaller forces to seize Brittany.

Sub-event_fulltext.Paragraph_34: Before the invasion, it had been thought necessary to divert a sizable U.S. force to capture the Breton ports, and plans had been formed to deploy not only the VIII Corps but also the XV, and possibly even the VII and XX.<sup>[30](https://www.ibiblio.org/hyperwar/USA/USA-E-Breakout/fn18.html#fn30)</sup> When German disorganization seemed so thorough, the opportunity of seizing Brittany with smaller forces became feasible.

Sub-events.Sub-event_summary: Patton plans to drive southwest to cut Brittany at its base, clear the peninsula, liberate regions, and reduce German defenses, with missions focused on clearing, securing ports, and eventual eastward drive.

Sub-event_fulltext.Paragraph_35: Specifically, General Patton planned to drive southwest from Avranches through Rennes to Quiberon Bay in order to cut the Brittany peninsula near its base and prevent the reinforcement or escape of German forces thus isolated.
Sub-event_fulltext.Paragraph_36: Next, he would clear Brittany by seizing the central plateau of the peninsula. In so doing, he would liberate a vast region of France, open interior lines of communication, and reduce the enemy defenses to isolated pockets along the coast. With the Germans penned into a few port cities, it would be relatively easy to force their capitulation. Once the ports were in American hands, the Third Army would be free to turn east, where the decisive battle of the European campaign would obviously be fought. Thus, Patton visualized his primary mission as clearing the peninsula, his incidental mission as securing Quiberon Bay and Brest first and the other ports later, his eventual mission as driving eastward toward Paris and the Seine.[31](https://www.ibiblio.org/hyperwar/USA/USA-E-Breakout/fn18.html#fn31)

Sub-events.Sub-event: Patton's Armored Columns and Task Force A
Sub-events.Sub-event_summary: Patton deploys 4th Armored Division to Quiberon, 6th to Brest, and Task Force A under Earnest to secure north shore railroad to Brest.

Sub-event_fulltext.Paragraph_37: Patton's method for securing Brittany was to unleash armored columns in the peninsula. The 4th Armored Division was to drive through Rennes to Quiberon. The 6th Armored Division was to go all the way to Brest. A third column, formed by activating a provisional unit called Task Force A under the command of Brig. Gen. Herbert L. Earnest, was to advance to Brest to secure the vital railroad that follows generally the north shore.<sup>[32](https://www.ibiblio.org/hyperwar/USA/USA-E-Breakout/fn18.html#fn32)</sup>

Sub-events.Sub-event: Importance of Brest Railroad and Bridges
Sub-events.Sub-event_summary: Task Force A tasked with capturing bridges on the railroad to Brest to ensure its condition; Grow instructed to protect Morlaix bridge.

Sub-event_fulltext.Paragraph_38: If Brest was to prove of value as a port of entry, the double-track railway linking it to Rennes had to be in good condition. Since the railroad crosses several big bridges that can not be quickly or easily replaced or repaired, Task Force A was to capture the bridges before the Germans could demolish them. That Patton considered this an important mission was clear when he requested General Grow of the 6th Armored Division also to keep an eye out for the bridges along the railroad, particularly the one at Morlaix.<sup>[33](https://www.ibiblio.org/hyperwar/USA/USA-E-Breakout/fn18.html#fn33)</sup>

Sub-events.Sub-event_summary: Patton views St. Malo as incidental, not assigning it as objective; influences Bradley to allow bypass if reduction too costly.

Sub-event_fulltext.Paragraph_39: Unlike General Bradley, General Patton considered the capture of St. Malo incidental to the entire Brittany campaign. He did not specifically assign it as an objective to any of his forces. And he apparently influenced Bradley to the extent that Bradley agreed St. Malo could be bypassed and contained if its reduction appeared to require too many forces and too much time.<sup>[34](https://www.ibiblio.org/hyperwar/USA/USA-E-Breakout/fn18.html#fn34)</sup>

Sub-events.Sub-event_summary: Patton's concept emphasizes distant objectives, exploitation of armor mobility and German disorganization, granting subordinates independence unlike methodical Cotentin approach.

Sub-event_fulltext.Paragraph_40: What emerged was a concept quite different from that which had governed operations in the Cotentin. Patton saw his immediate objectives far in advance of the front, for his intent was to slash forward and exploit not only the mobility and striking power of his armored divisions but also the German disorganization.<sup>[35](https://www.ibiblio.org/hyperwar/USA/USA-E-Breakout/fn18.html#fn35)</sup> Prone to give his subordinates free rein, Patton expected them to exercise independent judgment and tactical daring. Confident of the ability of armor to disrupt enemy rear areas and to sustain itself deep in enemy territory, and conscious of the weak and disorganized opposition, he felt that the ultimate objectives were immediately pertinent and attainable. There seemed little point in slowly reducing Brittany by carefully planned and thoroughly supervised operations unraveled in successive phases. As a result, Patton granted his subordinates a freedom of action that permitted the division commanders to be virtually independent.

Sub-events.Sub-event_summary: Patton transforms 6th Cavalry Group into Army Information Service for direct front-line reporting to maintain knowledge of changes, bypassing normal channels.

Sub-event_fulltext.Paragraph_41: With this concept of warfare that stressed taking advantage of the breaks, General Patton required constant knowledge of front-line changes. To get it, he renamed the 6th Cavalry Group (Col. Edward M. Fickett) the Army Information Service and transformed it into a communications unit. A varying number of reconnaissance platoons (each usually with two officers, twenty-eight men, six armored cars, and six jeeps) formed into troops under two squadrons were to report the activities of combat units down through battalion size. The reconnaissance platoons were to funnel G-2 and G-3 information through troop headquarters to squadron and group. The latter would co-ordinate and condense the information into teletype messages and send it directly to the army advance command post. Known as Patton's "Household Cavalry" and required to bypass normal communications channels, the 6th Cavalry Group was to provide a means of contact between far-flung forces engaged in diverse missions and the army command post, which was sometimes to be as much as a hundred miles behind the front.[36](https://www.ibiblio.org/hyperwar/USA/USA-E-Breakout/fn18.html#fn36) It thus happened on occasion that, though corps and divisions monitored the messages, the army staff was better informed on a particular situation than the corps directing the operation.

Sub-events.Sub-event_summary: Middleton, methodical, faces rapid changes in Brittany; plans two armored columns followed by infantry for orderly advances to objectives like Rennes and Dinan.

Sub-event_fulltext.Paragraph_42: In Brittany, the corps commander in immediate charge of operations, General Middleton, methodical and meticulous, found himself in a whirlwind that threatened to upset his ideas of orderly and controlled progress. The transfer of VIII Corps from First to Third Army brought changes in staff procedures, communications, and supply, but these were minor problems when compared to the exigencies that emerged in rapid succession as a result of the change from the positional hedgerow warfare in the Cotentin to wide-open exploitation in Brittany.
Sub-event_fulltext.Paragraph_43: General Middleton's plans for Brittany grew out of the premises that had governed the action in the Cotentin: orderly advances were to be made to specific objectives by units developing a compact fighting front. In conformance with this manner of operation, he planned to send two columns into Brittany--two armored divisions abreast, each followed by an infantry division--the same formation employed so successfully during the post-COBRA exploitation to Avranches. The 4th Armored Division, followed by the 8th Division, was to move southwest from Pontaubault and capture Rennes; the 6th Armored Division, supported by the 79th Division, was to strike westward from Pontaubault and seize in turn Pontorson, Dol-de-Bretagne, and Dinan. Once these objectives were secured, General Middleton would send his columns on to Quiberon and St. Malo, respectively. St. Malo, Middleton believed, was his "immediate task" in Brittany.<sup>[37](https://www.ibiblio.org/hyperwar/USA/USA-E-Breakout/fn18.html#fn37)</sup>

Sub-events.Sub-event_summary: Commanders like Grow and Earnest align with Patton's school, bypassing St. Malo; Wood and Grow feel affinity to Patton, units enthusiastic post-Avranches.

Sub-event_fulltext.Paragraph_44: The commanders who were to lead the spearheads into Brittany regarded themselves as belonging to the Patton school of thought. They seized upon the situation of exploitation with relish. Generals Grow and Earnest, who were to pass near St. Malo, for example, made no plans to capture the city, Earnest going so far as to tell his staff, with some exaggeration, that they would go by it without even looking at it.[38](https://www.ibiblio.org/hyperwar/USA/USA-E-Breakout/fn18.html#fn38)
Sub-event_fulltext.Paragraph_45: Generals Wood and Grow in particular felt toward General Patton, who, like them, was a tank officer, an affinity they could not feel toward General Middleton, bred in the infantry. They were convinced they understood better what Patton expected. Their units had been relatively untouched by the depressing combat in the hedgerows and had not sustained the heavy losses that were normal in the Cotentin. Having thrust victoriously to Avranches in the last days of July, they believed they had accomplished what other units had not been able to do. Having led the U.S. forces from the breakthrough into the breakout, the division commanders and their units became infected with an enthusiasm and a self-confidence that were perfectly suited to exploitation but proved to be a headache to those who sought to retain a semblance of control. A naturally headstrong crew became rambunctious in Brittany.
